prompt: A small amp is driven hard so a loud middle-frequency sine is clipped almost to a square wave with the same peak voltage. Assume a resistive load. Compared with the clean sine at that peak, roughly what happens to the average power?

options.explanation: Flattening the peaks keeps the waveform near its maximum for longer, raising the average power.

options.text: It roughly doubles; both the fundamental component and odd-harmonic power increase
options.explanation: Correct. A square wave at the same peak voltage dissipates twice the sine's average power into a resistor. Its fundamental amplitude is about 1.27 times that peak, so the added power is not all harmonics.
The waveform shape changes the average power even at the same peak.
Even a full square wave only doubles it.

workedExample:
1. A clean sine only touches its peak voltage briefly; on average its power is half its peak instantaneous power.
2. A square wave at the same peak voltage sits at that voltage all the time, so its average power is the full peak power: twice the sine's.
3. That extra power is not all harmonics: the square wave's fundamental is itself about 1.27 times the shared peak. But it also carries odd harmonics at a third, a fifth and a seventh of the fundamental's amplitude.
4. For a middle-frequency note, those harmonics fall in the tweeter's band, so the tweeter suddenly receives far more power than normal music would send it.
